newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Trichet calls for fiscal rectitude.
newsitem.headline: France's Trichet calls for fiscal rectitude.

text.p: Bank of France chief Jean-Claude Trichet warned the new Socialist government on Tuesday to stick to the path of fiscal rectitude and said structural economic reforms were vital to fighting record unemployment.

Sound monetary policy had brought interest rates to historic lows but was not enough to tackle France's 12.8 percent jobless rate, he told a news conference as he released the independent central bank's annual report.

Such action required structural reforms, sustained deficit reduction and controls on public spending, Trichet said, making the Bank's first major public statement since the Socialists ousted the centre-right in a parliamentary election on June 1.

"Structural reforms are imperative to increase employment," he said. Changes were needed in education, training and labour market flexibility, he said, and urged decision-makers to look beyond France's borders to seek ideas.
"We must be pragmatic and humble and look at what has worked elsewhere," he said, pointing to The Netherlands where the jobless rate of 5.7 percent is less than half that of France.
"The (Bank of France monetary policy) council can only hope the government, parliament, trade unions and employers implement these reforms in a pragmatic, unbiased way," he said.
He said the Bank's report had been written before Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's maiden speech to parliament last week and was not intended as a response.

Jospin announced a four percent rise in the national minimum wage and said he would end the previous government's efforts to cut the public work force, a sign some economists said might spell trouble for efforts to curb public deficits.

Trichet said he believed the single European currency, the euro, would be launched on schedule on January 1, 1999. But, in an apparent shift in emphasis, he shied away from saying France would strictly meet the Maastricht treaty goal of limiting public deficits to three percent of gross domestic product.
"He's being pragmatic," said one economist. "He's not the only one who may have moved his stance...More and more people are saying there's no point in hitting three percent on the nose."

Jospin said last week the government was committed to starting the single currency on time. But he also made no mention of meeting the deficit criteria precisely and Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn told parliament on Tuesday an audit of public finances ordered by the new government was likely to show a bigger than expected deficit.
Economists have said France might get away with a deficit of up to 3.5 percent of GDP but Germany would have difficulty accepting a deficit greater than that.

Newspapers have said France's deficit to GDP ratio could be between 3.3 and 3.8 percent this year without new spending cuts. The Socialists pledged during the elecion campaign not to implement new austerity measures to meet the Maastricht treaty goals.
Trichet's message on the need to keep cutting deficits and spending was "classic" and unsurprising, but the timing was important given the change of government, economists said.

Trichet said total public spending at 54.7 percent of GDP was "clearly too high," noting the European Union average was 49.9 percent and the average for the Group of Seven leading industrial nations was 39.7 percent.

He refused to be drawn on the new administration's policies. "We are not replying to the government's policy statement... But what we are saying is if one wants to create jobs, measures must be taken to reinforce competitiveness," he said.

In an interview with daily Le Monde, he said the markets were showing confidence in France despite the government's "less European and less strict line on the goal of deficit reduction" and attributed it to trust in the independent Bank.

Trichet said France's 10-year interest rates were the third lowest in the world because the franc was stable and credible and he promised the Bank would continue its efforts to ensure the new euro inspired as much confidence as the franc.
